abstract: The functions of genome regulatory proteins often emerge through long-term coevolution with their genomic and nuclear environments, complicating the distinction between intrinsic protein properties and context-dependent activities. The DNA-binding protein CTCF is a multifunctional regulator that plays central roles in genome organization and gene regulation across animals. Here, we investigated the behaviour of human CTCF in a deeply heterologous system by expressing it in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a lineage that diverged before the evolution of CTCF itself. Human CTCF was efficiently expressed, localized to the nucleus and associated with yeast chromatin, yet failed to establish robust sequence-specific binding or substantial transcriptional responses. Genome-wide analyses revealed no significant changes in chromatin accessibility, although modest footprinting and nucleosome-positioning effects were detected around predicted CTCF motifs. Together, our results suggest that chromatin association can occur independently of prior evolutionary history, whereas key aspects of CTCF target recognition and regulatory activity depend on long-term genome-protein coevolution.
